outcome: No proof or disproof of the Scholz inequality for all n has been found since 26 January 2024. The in-window events are a computer result from July 2024 that the stronger exact-equality form fails at a few n (the inequality holds strictly there), a conditional carry-degree bound (Agama, July 2024), a restricted-class result for 'complete numbers' (Agama, May 2025), and revisions of the author's 2021 arXiv paper (July 2024, March 2026) whose main inequality the paper itself calls 'slightly short of the original conjecture'. The latest source I could read treats the conjecture as open.
problem_asks: One universal claim over all n (sources state n >= 2): for every n, l(2^n - 1) <= n - 1 + l(n), where l(m) is the length of a shortest addition chain producing m. Parts: (a) l(2^n - 1), the shortest chain for a Mersenne number; (b) l(n), the shortest chain for the exponent; (c) the inequality between them with the additive term n - 1; (d) the claim is for all n, not for a family. The statement does not ask for the stronger exact-equality form l(2^n - 1) = n - 1 + l(n) studied in the Thurber and Clift literature, nor for Brauer's weaker bound, nor for bounds on l(2^n - 1) alone.

events.what_happened: E. G. Thurber, 'The Scholz-Brauer problem on addition chains', Pacific Journal of Mathematics 49(1), 1973. The journal page was not opened; the content below comes from a search extraction that dropped some inequality symbols. It proves a lower bound on l(n) for n with at least nine 1s in binary (l(n) >= floor(log2 n) + 4), treats a related conjecture for m = 3, and gives an infinite family n = 2^m * 23 + 7 with l(2n) = l(n).
events.delivers: Lower bounds on l(n) for n with many 1s, and an infinite family with l(2n) = l(n), per the extraction. As far as the extraction shows, nothing that establishes or refutes l(2^n - 1) <= n - 1 + l(n).
events.remains: The inequality for all n.

checked_by.who: Pacific Journal of Mathematics (journal of record)
checked_by.what_they_did: published the paper (listing seen in search results; article not opened)

events.doubts: Not read. The extraction dropped inequality symbols, so the exact lower-bound statement is unverified.
events.direction: Lower bounds and partial families; does not prove or refute the inequality as far as known.

events.what_happened: E. G. Thurber, 'Addition chains and solutions of l(2n) = l(n) and l(2^n - 1) = n + l(n) - 1', Discrete Mathematics 16 (1976) 279-289. Known from its title as cited in the Bielefeld bibliography and in Tall's preprint. Not opened.
events.delivers: Per its title only: solutions of the equality l(2^n - 1) = n + l(n) - 1 and of l(2n) = l(n). Any n satisfying the equality also satisfies the inequality at that n.
events.remains: The inequality for all other n.

checked_by.what_they_did: published the paper (inferred from citations; not opened)
checked_by.where: not located: no URL opened for this paper

events.direction: Per the title, supports the equality form at specific n, which would imply the inequality at those n.

events.what_happened: W. Aiello and M. V. Subbarao, 'A conjecture in addition chains related to Scholz's conjecture', Mathematics of Computation 61(203) (1993) 17-23. The AMS page returned HTTP 403, so the content below is from search extraction of the abstract and a secondary summary. The paper states that the Scholz conjecture's validity for all n is an open problem. It proposes that for every n there is a chain for 2^n - 1 of length l(n) + n - 1. It reports that this holds for all n <= 128 by computing chains, and for powers of 2.
events.delivers: Per the extraction: a conjecture stronger than the inequality (a chain of length exactly l(n) + n - 1 for 2^n - 1 would give the inequality), verified computationally for n <= 128 and proved for powers of 2. Establishes no general case of the inequality.
events.remains: The inequality for all n, and the stronger chain-existence conjecture for all n.

checked_by.who: Mathematics of Computation (AMS journal of record)
checked_by.what_they_did: published the paper (page returned HTTP 403; publication inferred from citations)

events.doubts: Content known only from search extraction and a secondary summary. Another search summary attributes the origin of the equality claim to Knuth and Thurber rather than to this paper (see disputes).
events.direction: Proposes a stronger conjecture that would imply the inequality; supports it computationally for small n.

events.what_happened: H. M. Bahig and K. Nakamula, 'Some properties of nonstar steps in addition chains and new cases where the Scholz conjecture is true', Journal of Algorithms 42(2) (2002) 304-316, with an erratum in J. Algorithms 47(1) (2003) 60-61. Title and erratum from the Bielefeld bibliography. Content from a search summary only; not opened.
events.revisions: Erratum published 2003 (Journal of Algorithms 47(1)); the erratum's content is not read.
events.delivers: Per a search summary: the inequality holds when the binary expansion of n has at most four 1s, and for infinitely many n with five 1s. The summary conflicts with Tall's account that all n with five 1s are covered (see disputes).
events.remains: The inequality for all n with six or more 1s, and the rest of the five-1s case per the summary.

checked_by.what_they_did: published the paper and an erratum (per bibliography; not opened)

events.doubts: Content unverified. The erratum's content is unknown, and the summary's claim about the five-1s case is not confirmed.
events.direction: Supports the inequality for the named classes (per summary).

events.what_happened: Neill Clift confirmed the inequality l(2^n - 1) <= n - 1 + l(n) for all n < 5,784,689 by computer. Flammenkamp's page dates the report to August 2005. The result was published as 'Calculating optimal addition chains', Computing 91(3) (2011) 265-284. Wikipedia and Agama's preprint report the same range.
events.revisions: Published in Computing 91(3) (2011) 265-284 per Agama's and De Koninck et al.'s citations; the DOI 10.1007/s00607-010-0118-8 appeared in search results and was not opened.
events.delivers: Checks finitely many instances (all n < 5,784,689) of the universal inequality. Gives no argument for larger n. Per Flammenkamp's page, the exact-equality form was also checked for n <= 64 by 2009.
events.remains: All n >= 5,784,689, and the general case.

checked_by.what_they_did: published the 2011 paper describing the computation

checked_by.qualification: maintains the shortest-addition-chain tables that Clift's computation uses
checked_by.what_they_did: reported Clift's result on his page and records that Clift checked his 1997 data (finding four l(n) errors)

events.doubts: A computer verification. The program and its correctness argument are not described in the pages I read. Flammenkamp's page records that Clift found four errors in the 1997 table, a data-quality issue that does not bear directly on this result.
events.direction: Supports the inequality for the checked range.

events.what_happened: Clift's progress on the exact-equality form l(2^n - 1) = n - 1 + l(n), as listed on Flammenkamp's page: August 2005 for n <= 28 and n = 30; December 2007 for n = 29; to May 2009 for n <= 64; May 2016 for n in {65, 66, 68, 72, 80, 96}; July 2018 for all n with l(n) <= 8 (new algorithm); July 2019 for n <= 134 with l(n) = 9; September 2019 for all n with l(n) = 9. The page states that equality 'is proved to hold at least for all n with l(n) <= 9'.
events.revisions: Successive steps through September 2019, as listed on the page. The page is undated beyond its footer.
events.delivers: Establishes the exact-equality form at the listed n, and for all n with l(n) <= 9 by the page's account. Each equality instance also satisfies the inequality at that n. Says nothing about the inequality for other n.
events.remains: The equality form for other n, and the inequality for all n.

checked_by.what_they_did: recorded Clift's steps on his page; no separate paper cited on the page

events.doubts: Web-page claims with no paper cited on the page for the 2016-2019 steps. Not independently verified.
events.direction: Consistent with the inequality; the equality form holds at the checked n.

events.what_happened: Amadou Tall, 'The Scholz conjecture on addition chain is true for v(n) = 4', Cryptology ePrint 2022/1160 (received and approved 6 September 2022). Claims the inequality for all integers whose binary expansion has exactly four 1s.
events.delivers: Proves the inequality for all n with exactly four 1s in binary. An infinite family of cases, not all n.
events.remains: All n with v(n) other than 4, including v(n) = 5, 6, 7 and above.
events.doubts: Unrefereed ePrint. Abstract read only (paraphrased), so the proof was not checked. No public review found in my searches. The author's later arXiv paper restates the v(n) <= 5 result citing prior work, which is not an independent check.
events.direction: Supports the inequality for v(n) = 4.

events.what_happened: Amadou Tall, 'The Scholz conjecture on addition chain is true for infinitely many integers with l(2n) = l(n)', arXiv:2210.13812, first posted 25 October 2022. The same title appears as Cryptology ePrint 2023/020 (received 5 January 2023, approved 9 January 2023). Per search results, it was published in Integers 24A (2024), the proceedings volume of the 2023 Integers conference, with publication dated 27 May 2024 in the PDF metadata. That date is from a search snippet and was not verified. The abstract says the conjecture is known for l(2n) = l(n) + 1, for v(n) <= 5, and for infinitely many n with v(n) = 6. It proves the conjecture for an explicit two-parameter family of v(n) = 7 integers, n = c1 * 2^(2m+k+3) + c2 with c1 = 5*2^(m+2) + 3, c2 = 3*2^(m+1) + 1, m >= 1, k >= 3, and for their doubles. The abstract says this family is Thurber's list.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only (25 Oct 2022). ePrint 2023/020 same title (Jan 2023). Journal publication Integers 24A, 2024 (per search snippet; the in-window date is the journal's, not the first argument's).
events.delivers: Proves the inequality for the explicit family of v(n) = 7 integers and their doubles, which gives infinitely many n with l(2n) = l(n) satisfying the inequality. The abstract says the family is Thurber's list of v(n) = 7 integers. The body I read does not enumerate Thurber's list.
events.remains: All other n: the rest of the v(n) = 7 integers, v(n) >= 8, and the v(n) = 6 cases beyond the known infinite set.

checked_by.who: Integers (electronic journal; proceedings volume of the 2023 Integers conference)
checked_by.qualification: peer-reviewed journal (the review process was not verified by me)
checked_by.what_they_did: accepted and published (received July 2023, accepted December 2023, published 27 May 2024, all per a search snippet of the PDF metadata)

events.directly_checkable: The family is explicit. Individual members can be tested by computing l for small parameter values, but the result itself is a proof by construction.
events.doubts: (i) The Integers PDF could not be read (binary), so the published statements and publication date are unverified. (ii) The arXiv abstract says the family is Thurber's list, but the body I read never enumerates Thurber's list, so that equivalence is unverified. (iii) Search summaries say the v(n) <= 6 case is known, which conflicts with the arXiv abstract (see disputes).
events.direction: Supports the inequality for these n. No counterexample is involved.
people: Amadou Tall (Universite Cheikh Anta Diop de Dakar, per the preprint)

events.what_happened: Amadou Tall, 'The Scholz conjecture for n = 2^m(23) + 7, m in N*', arXiv:2302.02143, first posted 4 February 2023. The abstract says the paper proves the conjecture for n = 2^m * 23 + 7, which Thurber gave as the first family with infinitely many n satisfying l(2n) = l(n). It also says the author will show the conjecture for Thurber's second family, given by an explicit sum of powers of 2 in parameters m and k. The body was not read.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only, per the abstract page.
events.delivers: Proves the inequality for the infinite family n = 2^m * 23 + 7. The abstract also says the second Thurber family is treated; this is not verified in the body.
events.remains: All other n.
events.doubts: Abstract only. A search summary attributes a journal version to this paper that I could not confirm.
events.direction: Supports the inequality for that family.

events.delivers: Unknown: not read. The title suggests a result restricted to star addition chains, which Brauer's bound already covers.
events.remains: Unknown from the title. Presumptively the inequality for all n.
events.doubts: Not opened. The title refers to a 'Third Conjecture' of Scholz, which may be a different statement. The venue's review standard was not checked.
events.direction: Unknown; the title suggests star-chain cases only.

events.delivers: Unknown: not read. The title claims a demonstration of a 'First Conjecture' of Scholz, which may or may not be the inequality.
events.remains: Unknown.
events.doubts: Not opened, and I could not confirm that the paper exists beyond the bibliography entry. If it claims the inequality for all n, it would be a claimed proof of an open problem in a venue whose review standard was not checked.
events.direction: Unknown.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, arXiv:2108.07720, first posted 8 August 2021. The title changed across versions. v1 is 'On the shortest addition chain of numbers of special forms'. Its abstract gives a crude bound iota(2^n - 1) <= n + 1 + G(n) and the weaker iota(2^n - 1) <= n + 1 + floor((n-2)/2), and does not mention Scholz. By v8 the title includes 'progress on the Scholz conjecture'. The latest version, v12 (28 March 2026, 35 pages), is 'On addition chains and progress on the Scholz conjecture'. v12 contains an unconditional Theorem 6.1: l(2^n - 1) <= n + 1 - sum_{j <= floor(log n/log 2)} xi(n,j) + 3 floor(log n/log 2) for n >= 4. It also has conditional Theorems 7.3-7.8 of the form l(2^n - 1) <= n - 1 + (1 + c') floor(log n/log 2) under a carry-degree hypothesis, and an open Conjecture 7.9 about carry degree. Per the v12 text the paper describes its main inequality as 'slightly short of the original conjecture'.
events.revisions: v2 18 Mar 2022; v3 5 Jun 2022; v4 28 Jul 2022; v5 1 Aug 2022; v6 20 Dec 2022; v7 9 Jan 2023; v8 6 Jul 2023 (first title with 'Scholz conjecture'); v9 17 Aug 2023; v10 27 Dec 2023; v11 24 Jul 2024; v12 28 Mar 2026 (comment: '35 pages; the paper has been massively reformatted and introduction expanded; ideas remain unchanged'). Dates are arXiv's. The v12 text I read covered about 100k of 123k characters plus the remaining 23k; the acknowledgements were not found.
events.delivers: Carry-based upper bounds on l(2^n - 1). The unconditional bound has an additive term of order floor(log n) beyond n + 1. The conditional bounds depend on a carry-degree hypothesis the paper does not prove. By the paper's own description the main inequality is slightly short of the original conjecture.
events.remains: The inequality for all n. The conditional part also depends on Conjecture 7.9 (carry degree of 2^n - 1).
events.doubts: Unrefereed arXiv preprint. Main results conditional on an unproved carry-degree hypothesis. Title and content were revised across versions. I read v1's abstract but not its body. A search summary reports an Academia Letters journal reference (June 2022) for an earlier version, which I did not verify. No published review found.
events.direction: Partial results toward the inequality. The paper does not claim to settle it and describes its main inequality as slightly short.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, 'On the Scholz conjecture on addition chains', Cryptology ePrint 2023/051 (received 16 January 2023; revised 8 July 2023). By the pothole method on factors of 2^n - 1, for all n >= 64: iota(2^n - 1) <= n + 1 - sum_{j=1}^{floor(log n/log 2)} xi(n,j) + 3 floor(log n/log 2), with 0 <= xi(n,j) < 1. The author says this is stronger than a general bound on iota(r) at r = 2^n - 1 and slightly weaker than the conjectured bound.
events.revisions: Revised 8 July 2023 per the ePrint page. The 'see all versions' page was not opened.
events.delivers: An unconditional bound for n >= 64. By the author's account it is slightly weaker than the conjectured inequality. It does not prove the inequality.
events.remains: The inequality for all n.
events.doubts: Unrefereed ePrint. The comparison with the conjectured bound is the author's own.
events.direction: Partial: an unconditional bound slightly weaker than the inequality for n >= 64.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, 'On the notion of carries of numbers 2^n - 1 and Scholz conjecture', Cryptology ePrint 2023/1959 (received 25 December 2023, approved 31 December 2023). Conditional results. If 2^n - 1 has carries of degree at most kappa(2^n - 1), built from floor(log n/log 2) and a fixed constant c > 0, then iota(2^n - 1) <= n - 1 + (1 + 1/(1+c)) floor(log n/log 2) for n >= 4. A generalisation with f(n) = o(log n) and f(n) -> infinity gives n - 1 + (1 + 2/(1+f(n))) floor(log n/log 2). The abstract does not compare these bounds with n - 1 + iota(n).
events.revisions: None listed on the page shown; 'see all versions' not opened.
events.delivers: Conditional bounds of the form n - 1 + O(log n) under a carry-degree hypothesis that is not proved. The abstract does not state the Scholz conjecture and does not show that the bound implies it. If the multiplier were 1, the bound would be at most n - 1 + iota(n), since iota(n) >= floor(log n/log 2). With a multiplier above 1 the implication depends on how the correction compares with iota(n), which the abstract does not say.
events.remains: The inequality for all n, and every n outside the carry-degree hypothesis.
events.doubts: Conditional on an unproved hypothesis. Unrefereed. The second theorem's hypothesis uses an unspecified function f(n).
events.direction: Supports the inequality only under hypotheses. No unconditional statement in the abstract.

events.what_happened: Neill Clift announced counterexamples to the exact-equality form l(2^n - 1) = n - 1 + l(n) in July 2024. Wikipedia dates it 'July 2024' and cites Clift's 'Exact Equality in the Scholz-Brauer Conjecture' on additionchains.com, retrieved 2024-07-20. Flammenkamp's page dates it 'On 1th July 2024' and says Clift 'disproved that the conjecture holds for all n'. The example given there: an addition chain of length 30978148 for 2^30978119 - 1, with l(30978119) = 31, so l(2^n - 1) < n - 1 + l(n). Wikipedia's example is n = 9307543, with l(n) = 29 and l(2^n - 1) <= 9307570 < 9307571 = n - 1 + l(n). The additionchains.com root page (opened) does not mention these numbers. The exact-equality subpage was not opened.
events.revisions: Wikipedia says the pages were retrieved 2024-07-20. The Clift exact-equality page is undated in what I could read. The day '1' is from Flammenkamp's page; Wikipedia gives only the month.
events.delivers: Shows that the exact-equality form fails at the stated n, where the inequality holds strictly. The two sources give different n (9307543 and 30978119) and I could not reconcile them. Restriction: it concerns only the equality form at those n. It says nothing against the inequality, which the listed chains satisfy.
events.remains: The inequality for all n, which is untouched. The equality form for all other n. The sources do not say whether other failures are known.
events.directly_checkable: Upper bound: the chain of about 3 * 10^7 steps for 2^30978119 - 1 can be checked by a program in principle, with numbers of about 30 million bits. The lower bound l(30978119) >= 31, which is needed to make the inequality strict, is an exhaustive computation and cannot be checked from the chain. The same split applies to n = 9307543.
events.doubts: Unrefereed web announcements. The primary page (Clift's exact-equality page) was not read, so I cannot say which n is the smallest counterexample or confirm the date. Flammenkamp's phrase 'disproved that the conjecture holds for all n' refers to the exact-equality form, not to the inequality, but it could be misread as a disproof of Scholz. Wikipedia describes it as 'not always tight'. No independent recomputation or paper found.
events.direction: Cuts against the exact-equality (stronger) form at the stated n. Does not cut against the inequality, which holds strictly at those n.
events.object: Explicit computer-found addition chains, not non-constructive. (a) A chain of length 30978148 for 2^30978119 - 1, with l(30978119) = 31 (Flammenkamp's page). (b) For n = 9307543, with l(n) = 29, a chain of length at most 9307570 for 2^n - 1 (Wikipedia). Neither chain is printed in the pages I read.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, 'On degrees of carry and Scholz's conjecture', Cryptology ePrint 2024/1199 (received 25 July 2024, approved 29 July 2024). Conditional result. If 2^n - 1 has carry degree at most kappa(2^n - 1) = (1/2)(l(n) - floor(log n/log 2) + sum_j {n/2^j}), then l(2^n - 1) <= n + 1 + sum_j ({n/2^j} - xi(n,j)) + l(n) for n >= 4. Category Applications, CC BY 4.0. The abstract makes no unconditional claim.
events.revisions: None listed on the page shown; the 'see all versions' page was not opened. The date is the approval date, used as a proxy for the posting date, which the page does not show.
events.delivers: Under a carry-degree hypothesis, an upper bound of the form n + 1 + l(n) + correction. Its excess over the conjectured n - 1 + l(n) is 2 + sum_j ({n/2^j} - xi(n,j)). The abstract does not show that this excess is at most 0. Restricted to n with the carry-degree hypothesis, and n >= 4.
events.remains: The inequality for all n, and every n outside the hypothesis.
events.doubts: Unrefereed. Conditional on a hypothesis that is not shown to hold for any infinite family in the abstract I read. The title names the conjecture but the abstract claims a bound, not the conjecture.
events.direction: Partial and conditional. Does not settle the inequality.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, 'On the gap between terms in an addition chain', Cryptology ePrint 2025/049 (received 13 January 2025, approved 14 January 2025). About how the gap between consecutive terms of a chain of length delta(n) ending at n is distributed. The page does not mention the Scholz conjecture or l(2^n - 1).
events.revisions: A 'current version' is mentioned on the page, with no version dates shown.
events.delivers: Nothing about l(2^n - 1) against l(n) + n - 1. A neighbouring question about the structure of chains.
events.remains: The whole problem.
events.direction: Not bearing on the problem.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, 'A note on closed addition chains and complete numbers', Cryptology ePrint 2025/833 (received 9 May 2025, approved 12 May 2025). Introduces a class of 'closed' addition chains. States that the numbers for which these chains are optimal satisfy the Scholz inequality iota(2^n - 1) <= n - 1 + iota(n). The class of 'complete numbers' is named in the title. Its definition was not visible: the PDF returned HTTP 403, and only the abstract page was read.
events.revisions: None listed on the page shown.
events.delivers: Per the abstract as read: the inequality for n in the class of numbers for which closed chains are optimal ('complete numbers'). A subclass defined by optimality of a special chain type, not all n. The class definition is unverified.
events.remains: The inequality for all n outside that class.
events.doubts: Unrefereed. The class is not defined in what I read. The claim can only be checked against the full PDF, which I could not open (HTTP 403).
events.direction: Restricted-class support for the inequality. No counterexample.

events.what_happened: Jean-Marie De Koninck, Nicolas Doyon and William Verreault, 'On the minimal length of addition chains', arXiv:2504.07332, first posted 9 April 2025. Studies F(m,r), the number of n in [2^m, 2^(m+1)) with l(n) <= m + r, with upper and lower bounds in the range r ~ cm/log m, extending Erdos's almost-all result. Its background section states the Scholz conjecture as l(2^(n+1) - 1) <= n + l(n+1), reports it verified for n <= 5,784,688 by Clift, and cites Tall for infinite families. It does not treat the inequality.
events.revisions: v1 only, per the abstract page.
events.delivers: Nothing about l(2^n - 1) against l(n) + n - 1. Results concern the distribution of l(n) over dyadic intervals, a different question.
events.remains: The whole problem.
events.doubts: Off-topic for the inequality. A third-party AI-generated review (themoonlight.io) lists 'Scholz conjecture' as a keyword of this paper. That review is a lead, not a source.
events.direction: Not bearing on the problem. It restates the conjecture and the Clift range.

events.what_happened: Jean-Marie De Koninck, Nicolas Doyon and William Verreault, 'On the distribution of the minimal length of addition chains', arXiv:2609.28374, submitted 23 September 2026. Abstract (read via the arXiv abstract page): counting functions F(m,r) and G(m,r) of integers in dyadic ranges by l(n) and by the number of distinct optimal chains, with matching bounds of the form K^r m^r, addressing a question of Erdos. The abstract does not mention the Scholz conjecture, l(2^n - 1), Brauer or Clift. The PDF is compressed and unreadable in the tool used, so the full text was not read.
events.revisions: v1 only, per the metadata read.
events.delivers: Nothing about the inequality per the abstract. A neighbouring distribution question.
events.remains: The whole problem.
events.doubts: Full text not read. A search snippet says its reference list includes Clift and Tall; I did not verify this. AI status: because the full text was not read, the none_found answer rests on the abstract alone.
events.direction: Not bearing on the problem.

disputes.summary: Which n with v(n) <= 6 are covered. The arXiv abstract of Tall's arXiv:2210.13812 says the inequality is known for v(n) <= 5 and for infinitely many n with v(n) = 6. Search summaries of the Integers version say it is known for all n with v(n) <= 6. The arXiv text is the primary source; the summaries are not, and the Integers PDF could not be read to settle it.

Bahig and Nakamula (2002), per a search summary, cover all n with four 1s and infinitely many with five 1s. Tall's preprint states that v(n) <= 5 is fully known. The two accounts differ on the five-1s case. The 2002 paper was not opened.

Clift's July 2024 result. Flammenkamp's page says Clift 'disproved that the conjecture holds for all n', which refers to the exact-equality form. Wikipedia says the bound is 'not always tight'. The listed chains are strictly shorter than n - 1 + l(n), so they satisfy the inequality. Read as a counterexample to the inequality, the result would be a misreading.

The n for Clift's 2024 example differs by source: Wikipedia gives n = 9307543 (l(n) = 29), Flammenkamp's page gives n = 30978119 (l(n) = 31). Both may be correct, as different examples, or one may be the smallest. Clift's primary page was not read.

Which 1993-era statement is the 'exact equality' conjecture. Aiello and Subbarao (1993) propose a stronger chain-existence conjecture verified for n <= 128. Thurber (1976, title only) and Clift's pages treat the equality l(2^n - 1) = n - 1 + l(n), with equality checked for n <= 64 and later for all n with l(n) <= 9. A search summary also attributes the origin of the equality claim to Knuth and Thurber, which I could not verify. The sources do not agree on which conjecture the 1993 paper states or verified.

Brauer (1939). Wikipedia says Brauer studied the conjecture and proved a weaker bound. Search summaries and Agama's preprint say Brauer proved the conjecture for star addition chains. These can both be true. Brauer's 1939 paper was not opened.

summary: I found no proof, disproof, or AI-attributed result for the Scholz inequality for all n in any source I could read, as of 13 October 2026. The record of events runs from the 1937 formulation (Scholz) through Brauer (1939), Thurber (1973, 1976), Aiello and Subbarao (1993), Clift's computation for all n < 5,784,689 (reported 2005, published 2011), Tall's families for v(n) = 4, the v(n) = 7 family, and n = 2^m * 23 + 7 (2022-2023), and Agama's carry-based bounds (arXiv 2021, revised through March 2026; ePrints 2023/051, 2023/1959, 2024/1199, 2025/833). The in-window events bearing on the problem are: (i) Clift's July 2024 counterexamples to the exact-equality form, at n = 30978119 (Flammenkamp's page) and/or n = 9307543 (Wikipedia), where the inequality holds strictly, so it does not touch the inequality; (ii) Agama's July 2024 conditional carry-degree bound, whose excess over n - 1 + l(n) the abstract does not show to be non-positive; (iii) Agama's May 2025 result for a class of 'complete numbers' whose definition I could not read; (iv) arXiv revisions of Agama's 2021 paper (v11 July 2024, v12 March 2026), whose author calls the main inequality 'slightly short of the original conjecture'. Neighbouring papers (De Koninck, Doyon and Verreault, April 2025 and September 2026; Agama, January 2025) concern the distribution of l(n) or gaps in chains and do not address the inequality. Close calls: (a) the July 2024 Clift result is labelled a 'disproof' on Flammenkamp's page; I read it as a counterexample to the equality form only, since the listed chains satisfy the inequality strictly. (b) Agama's 2024 and 2023 carry-degree bounds could imply the inequality on a carry-restricted class if the multiplier is at most 1, but the abstracts do not say so and the author's v12 calls the main inequality slightly short. (c) Tall's family result is described as covering Thurber's list of v(n) = 7 integers. I could not confirm this from the body, since the Integers PDF was unreadable. Verification and review: the only computation with a stated range is Clift's (n < 5,784,689), with no independent recomputation found and no formal (Lean or Coq) artifact found. Tall's 2022 work is recorded as published in Integers (per a search snippet, unverified). Agama's preprints have no public review found. No source names an AI system for this problem. My AI searches found nothing about addition chains or the Scholz conjecture in the AI-math announcements, trackers, or lab papers I checked. Four AI-related lists were not fully read (AlphaEvolve's 67 problems, AlphaProof Nexus's 44 OEIS conjectures, the GPT-5 science paper, and the 18-problem Gemini paper), so the AI answer is 'none found in what I could read'.
competing_reading: Read Flammenkamp's page at face value: 'Clift disproved that the conjecture holds for all n' (July 2024). A reader who takes 'the conjecture' to mean the Scholz inequality would record a 2024 disproof. The listed chains are strictly shorter than n - 1 + l(n), so they satisfy the inequality and refute only the equality form. A second reading: Agama's 2023/1959 and 2024/1199 bounds could imply the inequality for n satisfying a carry-degree hypothesis. The first bound has multiplier 1 + 1/(1+c), which exceeds 1, so it does not obviously imply the inequality; the second, with f(n) -> infinity, tends to n - 1 + floor(log n/log 2) <= n - 1 + l(n), but only if the hypothesis holds for the relevant n, which the abstract does not establish, and the author's v12 calls the main inequality slightly short. A third reading: Tall's v(n) = 7 family may be the whole of Thurber's list, which would close that case; I could not confirm this from the body. The judging pass would weigh whether any of these readings closes a part of the problem; none closes the statement for all n on what I read.
what_would_settle_it: (1) Clift's exact-equality page on additionchains.com, to fix the smallest counterexample to the equality form, the n values, and the date. (2) The Integers PDF of Tall's paper, to confirm the proven family, whether it is all of Thurber's list, the v(n) <= 5 and v(n) = 6 status, and the publication date. (3) The PDF of Agama's ePrint 2025/833, to read the definition of 'complete numbers' and the theorem. (4) Agama's arXiv 2108.07720 v12 Conjecture 7.9 and any proof that the carry-degree hypothesis holds for an infinite class, plus the paper's comparison of its bounds with n - 1 + l(n). (5) The texts of Aiello and Subbarao (1993), Thurber (1973, 1976), Bahig and Nakamula (2002, with erratum), and Brauer (1939). (6) Any refereed publication or expert write-up of Agama's Theorem 6.1 and its conditional results. (7) Any AI-lab, tracker, or paper result naming addition chains or the Scholz conjecture, and the full lists of the AlphaEvolve 67 problems and the AlphaProof Nexus OEIS conjectures.

event.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, 'A note on closed addition chains and complete numbers', Cryptology ePrint 2025/833 (received 9 May 2025, approved 12 May 2025). Introduces a class of 'closed' addition chains. States that the numbers for which these chains are optimal satisfy the Scholz inequality iota(2^n - 1) <= n - 1 + iota(n). The class of 'complete numbers' is named in the title. Its definition was not visible: the PDF returned HTTP 403, and only the abstract page was read.
event.revisions: None listed on the page shown.
event.delivers: Per the abstract as read: the inequality for n in the class of numbers for which closed chains are optimal ('complete numbers'). A subclass defined by optimality of a special chain type, not all n. The class definition is unverified.
event.remains: The inequality for all n outside that class.
event.doubts: Unrefereed. The class is not defined in what I read. The claim can only be checked against the full PDF, which I could not open (HTTP 403).
event.direction: Restricted-class support for the inequality. No counterexample.

judgement.why: The statement is the inequality for all n. Clift's July 2024 chains refute only the exact-equality form and satisfy the inequality strictly, so it is a variant, not a counterexample. Agama's carry-degree results are conditional on an unproved hypothesis (a reduction, scored none), and his unconditional bounds are by his own account weaker than the conjecture, so they settle nothing. Agama's v11/v12 arXiv revisions state 'ideas remain unchanged', so the 2021 paper stays pre-snapshot. The only post-snapshot event that could count is Agama 2025/833, scored as a case for a restricted class, unreviewed and doubtful because the class is undefined in what was read. Clift's equality checks for n with l(n) <= 9 cover finitely many n, so they are instances. Tall's Integers acceptance (December 2023) counts as journal digestion of a case. No AI involvement anywhere.
judgement.doubts: Agama 2025/833: whether 'complete numbers' form a meaningful infinite class or the result is close to tautological could not be judged; calling it a case rests on the abstract alone. The AI lists (AlphaEvolve, AlphaProof Nexus OEIS) were not fully read.
